kill_argument: The one thing new in this study's design is an equivalence test whose 2% bound is said to 'separate the two published readings'. The record misdescribes the literature that justifies that bound. -0.29 is called 'the least negative of the elasticities Clemens et al. report', but their revised paper reports -0.17 (QWI, one year, p. 12). The cited range of Clemens et al. QCEW estimates (-2.3 to -3.9) comes from the superseded 2025 version. The revision's two-year range, the horizon this study estimates, starts at -2.02, on the bound. Melo et al., whom the record cites, argue that QCEW 722513 tracks covered employment poorly across donor states, with divergence of -8 to +17 points, and that argument is absent from the limits. The 'separates the readings' claim holds for the medians, not the ranges. What I attacked that held: every round-1 finding. I fetched 13 new sources myself (all hashes match) and checked Crossref for 11 DOIs. The AB 257 dates, the Melo numbers, the Steier values, the DIR and EPI statements and the methods-paper passages are all correct. A web search found no causal study using 2026Q1. All remaining problems can be fixed by rewording.

findings.text: plan.json H2 calls the bound's wage effect 'the same pooled post-period estimand'. That is not so. Dube Table 1 Panel A SDID (+6.99) is the 2024Q2-2025Q3 average against a 2023Q4 base, with the outcome log emp/pop (Table 1 notes). The plan's estimand is 2024Q2-2026Q1 against a 2023Q3 base. Panel B, which the plan calls closest to its own timing, gives +6.71. The plan also describes -0.29 as 'the size of the more negative published estimates'. It is the least negative end of Clemens et al.'s one-year range, -0.29 to -0.49 (clemens2025did p. 11), and below the two-year 'just over -0.5' (clemens2026employment p. 12). The arithmetic (-0.02/0.07 = -0.29) is right.

findings.ruling: Not fixed; the new wording is wrong in a new way, and my round-1 remedy is partly to blame. I suggested 'the least negative of Clemens et al.'s estimates'. plan.json hypotheses[1] now says -0.29 is 'the least negative of the elasticities Clemens et al. report'. That is false. The revised paper, clemens2026employment p. 12 (section 4.2), says: 'The one-year estimated employment decline in the QWI translates into an elasticity of -0.17.' -0.29 is only the least negative of the one-year QCEW range in the July 2025 original (clemens2025did p. 11, -0.29 to -0.49). The 'close but not identical estimand' part of the fix is right. The parenthesis 'employment per capita' reads as though it describes the 7% wage effect. The wage row is log average weekly wage; only the employment outcome is per capita. Remedy: '-0.29, the least negative of the one-year QCEW elasticities in Clemens, Edwards and Meer (2025)' (or cite the revised -0.40 / 'just over -0.5'), and move 'employment per capita' so that it qualifies the employment outcome.

findings.text: The H2 bound sentence quotes the wrong Clemens et al. range for the claim it supports. plan.json hypotheses[1] says 'the QCEW estimates Clemens et al. report (about -2.3% to -3.9%) lie beyond -2%; a CI inside +/-0.02 therefore excludes the Clemens et al. QCEW reading'. -2.28 to -3.93 is the one-year range of the superseded July 2025 version (clemens2025did Table 1 Panel B). The question cites the revised w34033. The revision's one-year range is -2.19 to -3.90 (Table 1 Panel B). Its two-year range, the horizon of this study's eight-quarter estimand, is -2.02 to -5.03 (Table 3 Panel B; claim c-cemn2026). So the least negative two-year Clemens et al. QCEW estimate (DDD vs rest of US, -2.02%, about -0.0204 log points) sits on the bound. A CI inside +/-0.02 excludes it only by rounding. The contribution's 'an equivalence test against a 2% bound that separates the two published readings' is therefore true of the Clemens et al. median (-3.45) and detrended cells, not of the whole range. Also, the revision puts the two-year wage differential at 'just over 6 percent' (clemens2026employment p. 11). With that first stage, -0.02 corresponds to an elasticity of about -0.33, not -0.29.

findings.text: Melo et al.'s central QCEW argument is recorded as a claim (c-melo-coverage) but is not carried into the plan's limits or threats. The paper says its classification findings 'cast doubt on previous efforts to measure the effects of AB 1228 using QCEW data stratified at the' six-digit level (p. 16). It also says that 'QCEW employment counts among limited-service restaurants may be a poor proxy, both as point-in-time estimates and approximations of longitudinal trends' (p. 19). It adds that 'every state other than California is a potential donor, so state-specific measurement divergence of this size can distort the counterfactual' (p. 19). The divergence they report, 2019-2025 QCEW-minus-YTS changes from -8 to +17 points across states, is far wider than this study's 2-point equivalence bound. plan.json contribution (limits) mentions only dilution and misfiling into 722511/722515. T9 and T10 cover the same two points and the classification change (rob-7225). None says that donor states' QCEW 722513 trends may diverge from covered-chain trends, or that Melo et al. read their evidence as undermining QCEW 722513 designs. YTS is modelled data and Melo et al. say it is not definitively accurate, so this is a contested measurement objection, not a known bias. A referee will still raise it, and the record does not answer it.
findings.evidence: claims.jsonl c-melo-coverage; plan.json contribution ('Limits known now'), design.threats T9-T10; melo2026covered pp. 16, 18-19, Figure 5.
findings.remedy: One sentence in the limits (and in T10): Melo et al. argue that QCEW 722513 may track covered-chain employment poorly over time and across donor states (2019-2025 divergence -8 to +17 points, against YTS, itself modelled data); the estimand is defined on QCEW 722513, and the paper does not claim it equals the effect on covered establishments.

The same page (steier2026recordinglaw, which I fetched; the sha256 prefix f7743d164afc19d6 matches) also publishes 2026Q1 average weekly pay indexed to 2023Q3: 114.8 for California against 104.3 for the rest of the US. sources/notes.md section 2, which the PI's brief relies on, quotes those two numbers. The damage is small, because H1 is a one-sided first-stage test that the published 7-8% wage effects already predict. The disclosure should still be complete.

findings.text: AB 257 (the FAST Recovery Act), enacted September 2022, set up a Fast Food Council that could raise the wage of chains with 100+ locations to as much as $22 in 2023. A referendum petition stayed it in January 2023, and AB 1228 replaced it in September 2023. Three cited sources describe this: sosinskiy2026effects p. 7 ('This earlier law, passed in September 2022 ... as high as $22'; 'in January 2023 a state court stayed the implementation'), hamdi2025wage p. 6 and fn 7, and melo2026covered Section 2.1 pp. 5-6. The crew's record never mentions it (grep for 'AB 257' or 'FAST Recovery' in plan.json, claims.jsonl and sources/notes.md returns nothing). plan.json H2 calls 2023Q3 'the last quarter before the law was signed' and builds the primary-specification selection rule and the MDE from pre-2023Q3 data. It names Dube Table 1 Panel B (base 2022Q1-2023Q3) as the published result closest to its timing. All three use quarters in which a higher sectoral wage was law (2022Q3-2023Q1) or pending a referendum (2023Q1-2023Q3). No cited source estimates an AB 257 anticipation effect, so the size of the problem is unknown, but it is a known threat the record omits.

findings.text: The record cites melo2026covered only for its SDID coefficients (c-melo2026). It leaves out the paper's two QCEW findings, both of which bear on this study's outcome and comparison sector. (a) Misclassification (Section 3.1.1, p. 15 and fn 20): in Louisiana QCEW, only 77.7% of matched fast-food chain locations are coded 722513, 9.2% are coded 722515 and 7.9% 722511, and 14% of chains have locations in both 722513 and another restaurant code. Melo et al. warn that classification may change when the policy changes the mix of establishments. plan.json names only 722515 as unusable as a control. 722511, a candidate DDD sector in the literature and a fetched slice (dr-fetch), therefore also holds covered establishments. (b) Coverage (p. 19, PDF p. 21, and Figure 4): in California in 2025, employment at chains with 60+ locations (YTS) is 33% below QCEW 722513 employment. This is an imperfect but published approximation of the covered share, from a different universe that also includes some 722515 chains. It contradicts plan.json's 'the share for 722513 alone is not known' and sources/notes.md 6.2's 'not a sourced number'. Figure 5 also shows that the YTS-QCEW gap changes from 2019 to 2025, which Melo et al. note can bias DD designs.

findings.remedy: Add citation claims for (a) and (b). Reword the coverage limit to say a YTS-based comparison puts covered-chain employment at about two-thirds of QCEW 722513 in California, with Melo et al.'s caveats. State in the limits that 722511 contains covered chains, so a DDD against it is contaminated in both directions.

One wording point: Melo et al. do not say the YTS universe includes 722515 chains; I record that only as a possibility suggested by the Louisiana shares. The plan.json limits sentence is the PI's to reword. PI: plan contribution now uses Melo et al.'s coverage figure and names 722511 and 722515 as unclean controls.

findings.text: The design H1-H2 commits to has no verified source in refs.bib or sources.json. H1 requires inference 'valid with a single treated state (Ferman-Pinto, conformal, or a permutation ...)'. H2's candidate set includes synthetic control and SDID, and its decision rule is a two one-sided test. The selection rule picks a specification by placebo-in-time fit. None of Ferman and Pinto (2019, REStat; cited by Dube), Arkhangelsky et al. (2021, AER), Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010), Abadie (2021, JEL, on in-time placebos and feasibility), Chernozhukov, Wuthrich and Zhu (2021, JASA, conformal), Conley and Taber (2011) or an equivalence-testing reference (e.g., Schuirmann 1987) is recorded. The most relevant omission is Ferman, Pinto and Possebom (2020, JPAM), 'Cherry picking with synthetic controls', which w35931 cites. It studies specification searching in exactly this kind of choice and bears directly on whether the RMSE selection rule protects against it. The design gate will turn on whether the chosen inference reaches its nominal level with about 20 or 48 donors, and that claim needs its source's assumptions, such as Ferman-Pinto's heteroskedasticity correction by group size.

July 2021), abadie2010synthetic (NBER w12831), abadie2021using (JEL as printed), chernozhukov2021exact (arXiv v10), ferman2020cherry (MPRA WP), conley2011inference (NBER t0312), and for TOST schuirmann1987comparison (PubMed abstract) and lakens2017equivalence (PMC full text). One claim each (c-ferman-pinto, c-sdid-placebo, c-adh-placebo, c-abadie-guidance, c-conformal, c-cherry-picking, c-conley-taber, c-tost). notes.md section 9 gives each method's one-treated-unit assumptions with pages: FP's scale-only heteroskedasticity and N0 -> infinity, simulated with 25 groups (21 states is fewer); SDID placebo needs homoskedasticity across units; ADH rank p-values need California first of 21 for p = 0.048; conformal needs many stationary pre-periods; FPP show fit-based specification choice still over-rejects, and the note says how far the plan's pre-2019 placebo-RMSE rule differs from what they studied.
findings.ruling: Fixed. Nine methods sources recorded. I checked a sample against the documents, which I fetched myself; every sha256 prefix matches sources.json. ferman2020cherry: 14.3 percent with T0 = 12 and seven specifications (MPRA PDF p. 17), and over-rejection 'even when we restrict the set of choices to specifications with a good pre-treatment fit' (PDF p. 6). abadie2010synthetic: California's MSPE ratio rank '1/39 = 0.026', in-time placebos 'for cases in which the number of available comparison regions is small', and fn 4 on anticipation (w12831). abadie2021using: 'Safeguard against Specification Searches' on journal p. 406, volatility and no anticipation on p. 409, backdating on pp. 410 and 414 (PDF page + 390). ferman2019inference: checked in design-r1. Crossref metadata for ferman2019, ferman2020, ferman2021, conley2011, chernozhukov2021, abadie2021, schuirmann1987 and lakens2017 matches refs.bib (title, journal, volume, issue, pages).

findings.text: The novelty claim c-no-2026-qcew ('No study of AB 1228 found uses QCEW data for any 2026 quarter') and plan.json's 'the data add one preliminary quarter, 2026Q1' leave out a public analysis that already uses 2026Q1. Recording Law, 'Data Story' on AB 1228, by Adam Steier, published 6 November 2026 and audited 16 November 2026 (https://www.recordinglaw.com/data-stories/california-20-fast-food-wage-data/), uses QCEW NAICS 722513 monthly employment 'through the first quarter of 2026 (released August 28, 2026)'. It reports California at 97.06 against 98.99 for the rest of the US in March 2026 (September 2023 = 100), California 1.65% below its March 2024 level against 0.90% for the rest of the US. It runs no DD and makes no causal claim. So the narrow claim (no causal or pre-specified estimate uses 2026Q1) still stands. But 'no study uses' 2026 data is not safe as written, and the raw post-period contrast for the one new quarter is public. This matters for the 'pre-specified, not blind' disclosure in plan.json's contribution.

findings.text: Other obvious prior work is missing from the record: Card and Krueger (1994), the reference fast-food minimum-wage study; Wiltshire, McPherson, Reich and Sosinskiy (2024, JLE forthcoming), on California fast-food employment under the earlier $15 phase-in and the closest prior evidence for this state and sector (cited by Sosinskiy-Reich); Dube, Reich, Bhatt and Sosinskiy (2024) on restaurant employment; Cengiz et al. (2019); and Neumark and Rodriguez-Lopez (2026), cited by w34033. Also missing are Clemens, Edwards, Meer and Nguyen (2026a, NBER w34990, March 2026, prices), which reports prices rising between enactment and implementation and attributes part of the rise to spillovers to full-service restaurants (abstract and p. 1), relevant to anticipation and to the 722511 comparison, and Thornberg (2025, Pepperdine/Beacon), cited by Melo et al. for revisions to the preliminary California data, relevant because 2026Q1 is preliminary. Reich and Sosinskiy (2024, IRLE WP 104-24) is listed as 'not reached' in notes.md 8, but it is available at https://irle.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Sectoral-Wage-Setting-in-California-09-30-2024.pdf.

findings.text: c-ab1228-no-increase says the MW-2025 and MW-2026 orders 'still list the fast-food rate as the one effective April 1, 2024'. The orders list no fast-food rate. They name fast-food employers 'effective April 1, 2024' and refer to separate supplements (MW-2026 lines on 'Supplements to this order ... are available online').
